findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The HRA budget includes a £249,000 increase in interest paid, which the paper attributes to the repayment of a fixed-term loan.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: No provision for Local Government Reorganisation costs is included in the draft budget, and the paper says the financial implications are not yet sufficiently developed.
findings.detail: The paper says reorganisation costs are not yet quantified, and that provision for them was made through the minimum reserves assessment approved for the current year. It states a separate budget decision will be brought forward once the scope, governance and resource requirements are clearer.
findings.matters: A finance director at a council facing reorganisation will want to see whether costs are being held in reserves, budgeted, or left unquantified, and how that choice affects the position the council hands to a successor authority.
findings.figures: No LGR provision in the 2027/28 draft budget; reorganisation provision is held within the minimum reserves assessment
findings.quote: No provision has been included within the draft budget for additional costs associated with Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The Solar Canopy capital bid, costed at £2,225,840, was classed as unaffordable because the return on investment is not viable over its payback period.
findings.detail: Table 15 lists the Solar Canopy costing at £2,225,840 among capital bids categorised as unaffordable, with the comment that the return on investment is not viable due to extensive payback periods. The paper notes that the bid was requested by members during budget setting, and that business cases were judged unaffordable due to no income generation or time recovery of costs.
findings.matters: A finance director weighing an energy or income-generating capital scheme will see the paper's reasoning, which turns on payback and not on the scheme's merit.
findings.figures: Solar Canopy costing £2,225,840; total of the capital bids categorised unaffordable is not stated in the paper
findings.quote: Solar Canopy Costing £2,225,840 Blue ROI not viable due to extensive pay back periods

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The Derbyshire finance officers did not recommend a 2027/28 business rates pool, concluding the potential gains were limited and outweighed by the risk of losses.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the Derbyshire Finance Officers Association met on 4 November 2026 to consider a business rates pool. Its conclusion was that none of the authorities had significant business rates growth above forecast, so the potential gains were limited and outweighed by the risk of losses, and the council has not entered a pool for 2027/28.
findings.matters: Pooling decisions in a two-tier or reorganising county area change the business rates retention a council carries, and peers considering the same MHCLG invitation will want to see the reasoning.
findings.figures: Pool applications closed 9 November 2026; DFOA met 4 November 2026
findings.quote: the potential financial gains from a 2027/28 Derbyshire Business Rates Pool gains were limited and were outweighed by the risk of losses.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The draft HRA budget shows a 2027/28 deficit of £186,679, with HRA general reserves projected to fall from £3,068,000 in March 2027 to £1,274,000 in March 2028.
findings.detail: The paper states the draft HRA budget is a deficit of £186,679 for 2027/28 and that HRA general reserves are projected to remain above the £1m minimum. Table 14 shows the reduction is driven by a planned use of reserves of £1,794,000 in 2027/28, and the paper says continued absorption of non-core services would reduce reserves further and require corrective action.
findings.matters: A landlord's general reserves falling toward a minimum floor while capital needs rise is a position lenders and peer HRA finance teams track closely.
findings.figures: 2027/28 HRA deficit £186,679; HRA general reserves £3,068,000 (March 2027) and £1,274,000 (March 2028); planned use of reserves 2027/28 -£1,794,000; minimum reserve balance £1m
findings.quote: The draft budgeted position for the 2027/28 year is estimated to be a deficit position of £186,679 as set out in Appendix 3.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The Medium-Term Financial Plan projects a deficit of £3,878,062 in 2028/29 after the leisure centre interest capitalisation, which the paper describes as a structural funding gap.
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFP continues to identify a structural funding gap in future years, and that further action is needed for long-term sustainability. Table 2 shows the Nov 26 projected gap for 2029/30 at £7,159,177 and for 2030/31 at £6,959,183, with a total five-year gap of £20,030,346.
findings.matters: Finance directors at peer councils and lenders assess whether a plan without identified measures for later years is credible, and this paper states it has none yet identified as firm.
findings.quote: Despite this progress, the MTFP continues to identify a structural funding gap in future years, with a projected deficit of £3. 878 million in 2028/29 after allowing for the capitalisation of leisure centre borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The 2027/28 General Fund gap of £1,931,289 is to be balanced through the use of reserves, with General Fund reserves falling from £10,361,413 in April 2026 to £8,102,125 by March 2028.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states that the 2027/28 budget gap is to be balanced through reserves. Table 12 projects General Fund unallocated reserves of £10,361,413 at April 2026, £10,033,413 at March 2027 and £8,102,125 at March 2028, with total useable revenue reserves at £20,742,951 by March 2028.
findings.matters: Balancing a year's budget from reserves is a direct draw on the financial buffer that lenders and peers use to judge resilience, and the paper's own projections show how far it falls.
findings.figures: 2027/28 gap £1,931,289; General Fund reserves £10,361,413 (April 2026), £10,033,413 (March 2027), £8,102,125 (March 2028); total useable revenue reserves £20,742,951 (March 2028)
findings.quote: a revised budget gap position of £1.931 million to be balanced through the use of reserves.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: Capitalising the Leisure Centre's construction interest under IAS 23 reduces the 2027/28 General Fund revenue cost by £1,750,006.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the main reduction in revenue costs since September to the intended adoption of IAS 23, which allows interest incurred during asset construction to be capitalised. The paper states this can only apply until the asset is in use, so borrowing in 2027/28 is capitalised until completion in 2028/29, and the final figure will be reported in February 2027.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere will want to know that a large part of a council's improved position depends on an accounting policy and on a construction timetable, rather than on recurring savings.
findings.figures: £1.750m capitalised interest saving in 2027/28 (paragraph 4.8); £1,750,006 in 2027/28 and £875,003 in 2028/29 (Table 11)
findings.quote: The main driver of the decrease in revenue costs is the intended adoption of accounting policy IAS 23, which allows for the capitalisation of interest costs incurred whilst a new asset is in construction.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The Sustainable Finance Plan recorded £630,023 of savings in 2026/27 against a target of £1,845,000, after exceeding its 2025/26 target.

findings.paper_title: CONSOLIDATED DRAFT BUDGET REPORT 2027-28 AND MEDIUM-TERM FINANCIAL PLAN TO 2031-32
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget outturned as balanced after the Budget Optimisation Board's work, which delivered £1.65 million of savings against the predicted 2026/27 gap.
findings.detail: The paper says the Budget Optimisation Board delivered £1.65 million of savings to address the predicted 2026/27 budget gap, and that the year then outturned as balanced. The Feb 2023 MTFP had forecast a 2026/27 deficit of £3.340m, and the latest forecast is a deficit/(surplus) of (£0.102m).
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the forecast gap against the outturn and the savings route used to close it, which is a direct test of the savings plan.

findings.quote: As a result of the Board 2026/27 out turned a balanced budget position.

findings.headline: Personnel/HR forecast is £58k adverse, with medical fees of £50k linked to increased counselling usage, and an Employee Assistance Scheme cost pressure of £25k
findings.detail: The paper reports medical fees of £50k adverse from increased use of counselling services, and an approved cost pressure of £25k for the Employee Assistance Scheme. The mitigation is a self-referral employee assistance programme intended to reduce use of the counselling service.
findings.matters: Rising counselling usage among staff is a wellbeing and cost pressure that HR-linked budgets at other councils may also see.
findings.figures: £64k adverse (Organisational Development); £58k adverse (Personnel/HR); £50k medical fees; £25k Employee Assistance Scheme cost pressure
findings.quote: Medical Fees - £50k due to increased usage of counselling services.

findings.headline: Legal Services forecast £71k adverse on vacancies, with agency costs of £115k and external legal charges of £80k, and the council is exploring market supplements
findings.detail: Legal Services salaries are reported as £135k adverse because of vacant posts, offset by £115k of agency costs and £80k of external legal charges. The paper says the council is exploring market supplements to attract applicants, which it expects to remove the need for agency and reduce external legal consultancy.
findings.matters: Recruitment difficulty in legal services, with agency and external counsel costs replacing in-house posts, is a pressure other councils will recognise as a driver of their own legal spend.
findings.figures: £71k adverse (Legal Services); £135k adverse salaries; £115k agency costs; £80k external legal charges
findings.quote: Exploring market supplements to attract applicants which will remove the need for agency and greatly reduce external legal consultancy costs.

findings.headline: Planning development control income is forecast £379k above budget as the council receives more planning applications, with the Local Plan allocations cited
findings.detail: The paper attributes a favourable £300k variance in Dealing with Development Control Applications to increased planning applications, including two strategic allocations in the 2026/27 Local Plan submission and further allocations in Part 2 of the Local Plan. It notes the council expects this activity to continue, and additional consultancy cover was needed.
findings.matters: The paper links a planning income gain directly to the Local Plan timetable, which other councils planning strategic allocations would want to test against their own application pipelines.
findings.figures: £379k favourable income; £300k favourable net variance (Dealing with Development Control Applications)
findings.quote: Two strategic allocations in the local plan submitted in 2026/27 along with additional strategic allocations due during part 2 local plan stage starting September which contribute to increased applications

findings.headline: Business rates forecast revised upwards on expected growth from the South Derbyshire Logistics and Energy Park at Drakelow, with appeals provision still uncertain
findings.detail: The paper says officers have revised the business rates forecast to reflect favourable movement in anticipated growth, particularly from the Drakelow Logistics and Energy Park. Appeals are described as a significant area of uncertainty, linked to the 2023 rating list deadline, and a further update will come at Q3.
findings.matters: Business rates growth from a single strategic site and an unresolved appeals provision are both points other councils with similar growth schemes would weigh in their own retained-rates forecasting.
findings.figures: Retained Business Rates £3,446k in both budget and forecast; the revised growth figure is not stated in the paper
findings.quote: appeals continue to present a significant area of uncertainty with values increasing because of  the deadline associated with the 2023 rating list.

findings.headline: Capital programme spend at Q2 is £2.745m, with the General Fund at £1.689m and HRA at £1.056m against a total forecast budget of £26.885m
findings.detail: The paper reports Q2 capital spend of £2.745m across both accounts. The General Fund forecast budget is £22.255m against an approved £13.954m, and total capital expenditure is forecast at £26.885m against £17.904m approved. Several schemes are expected to slip, including HRA vehicle replacements (£780k delayed).
findings.matters: A capital programme forecast sitting well above the approved budget at mid-year is a signal of re-profiling and funding decisions that other councils delivering similar schemes would compare.
findings.figures: £2.745m Q2 spend; £1.689m General Fund spend; £1.056m HRA spend; £26.885m total forecast; £17.904m approved budget; £8.981m variance

findings.headline: Pay award of 3.3% for 2026/27 exceeds the 3.2% built into the General Fund and HRA budgets, with the difference funded from reserves
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 pay award was agreed at the end of August at 3.3%, against 3.2% built into the budgets. The paper states that the resulting overspend will be funded from General Fund and HRA reserves.
findings.matters: A small pay-award overshoot drawn from reserves is a common pressure that finance officers at other councils will be tracking against their own 2026/27 settlements.
findings.figures: 3.3% pay award; 3.2% built into budgets
findings.quote: The pay award for staff for 202 6/27 was agreed at the end of August at 3.3%.

findings.headline: Council seeks £80,000 supplementary estimate from General Fund reserves to fund external consultancy and temporary capacity for a move to a Cabinet governance model
findings.detail: The paper states that the council is now required to implement the transition to Leader and Cabinet governance, having been exempt while in the LGR process. The £80,000 one-off sum would fund external consultancy, constitutional review, temporary project capacity and specialist advice. The Monitoring Officer says the council must adopt a Cabinet model by June 2027.
findings.matters: The council is drawing a one-off, non-recurring sum from reserves to meet a statutory governance transition, a cost that other councils moving from committee systems would need to budget for.
findings.figures: £80,000 supplementary estimate from General Fund reserves; deadline June 2027
findings.quote: The Council is required to adopt a Cabinet Model by June 2027 as it is no longer part of the LGR programme.

findings.headline: Vehicle hire problems with the new twin-pack RCV fleet are being pursued with Dennis Eagle for compensation, with the discussions ongoing
findings.detail: The paper says reliability issues with the new twin-pack RCV fleet have caused additional vehicle hire costs. Discussions with the manufacturer about appropriate compensation are ongoing, and the wider fleet replacement plan is to be reviewed after appointment of a new Head of Operational Services.
findings.matters: Warranty or compensation claims against a supplier for a fleet failure are a recoverable-cost question that other councils buying similar RCVs would need to understand.
findings.figures: Not separately quantified in the paper
findings.quote: Discussions are ongoing with Dennis Eagle regarding appropriate compensation.

findings.headline: HRA forecast is a £343k deficit against a £211k budgeted deficit, with responsive repairs overspend of £734k partly offset by a £615k favourable planned maintenance position
findings.detail: The paper reports the HRA forecast deficit at £343k against a budgeted £211k. The responsive repairs (DLO) overspend of £734k is attributed to agency costs and Awaab's Law-related repairs of £650k. Planned maintenance is forecast £615k favourable through use of a reserve to fund planned maintenance costs.
findings.matters: A reserve-funded offset of a responsive repairs overspend is a pattern finance directors managing HRA repairs under Awaab's Law pressures would compare against.
findings.figures: £211k budgeted HRA deficit; £343k forecast HRA deficit; £132k adverse movement; £734k responsive overspend; £650k anticipated Awaab's law costs; £615k favourable planned (HRA revenue)
findings.quote: R&M - £650k - anticipated costs associated with Awaabs law.

findings.headline: Leisure Centre forecast 2026/27 expenditure revised down from £15.8m, with works started on site after S106 and planning delays
findings.detail: The paper reports the Leisure Centre project has moved into delivery with works commenced on site, but the 2026/27 forecast has been reduced from the previously assumed £15.8m. The paper attributes this to a later than anticipated start caused by the complexity of the S106 Agreement and other planning matters, and to long lead-in items ordered late.
findings.matters: A £15.8m forecast reduction on a single scheme is a large in-year slippage that feeds directly into the investment income gain reported elsewhere in the paper.
findings.figures: Q2 spend £482,108; Q2 forecast expenditure £7,336,336; previous assumption £15.8m (£15,852,266 budget); variance -£8,515,930
findings.quote: The forecast expenditure for 2026/27 has been revised down from the previously assumed £15.8m, reflecting the later than anticipated start on site due to the complexity of the S106 Agreement and other planning matters

findings.headline: Interest and investment income is forecast £226k favourable, with the council investing with other local authorities at 4.3% against a 3.7% Q1 assumption
findings.detail: The paper attributes higher-than-budgeted investment income to slippage on the Leisure Centre spending, which left cash balances higher and allowed further lending to other local authorities. The base rate is stated as 3.75% against 3% assumed from Arlingclose.
findings.matters: The paper ties an investment income gain directly to capital slippage, a link finance directors managing cash balances against capital delays would want to see quantified.
findings.figures: £226k favourable (General Fund interest and investment income); 4.3% achieved against 3.7% Q1 basis; base rate 3.75% vs 3% anticipated
findings.quote: Interest rates at Q1 were based on 3.7%, however 4.3% has been achieved.

findings.headline: Garden and food waste disposal recycling credits claim for April and May not yet refused, £178k additional cost if unsuccessful
findings.detail: Garden waste disposal responsibility passed to Derbyshire County Council from April 2026 while the Biffa contract was extended to June 2026. The council has submitted a recycling credits claim for April and May, and the paper says there is no indication payment will be refused. If the claim fails there would be an additional £178k cost, not reflected in the outturn.
findings.matters: The shift of garden waste disposal responsibility between tiers and the recycling credit mechanism is a transition risk other two-tier councils may be facing with the same county arrangements.
findings.figures: £178k potential additional cost; April and May claim period
findings.quote: Should the claim not be successful, there would be an additional cost of £178k, which has not been reflected in the current outturn.

findings.headline: Waste service turnover has been 20–25% of the refuse workforce over the past 12 months, with agency costs remaining high
findings.detail: The paper reports that approximately 20–25% of the refuse workforce left the organisation in the past year, which it links to increased vacancies and continued reliance on agency staff to maintain statutory waste collection.
findings.matters: Workforce attrition at this scale is a staffing-capacity and cost issue that other councils running statutory waste services would recognise as a driver of agency spend.
findings.figures: approximately 20 –25% of the refuse workforce leaving over the past 12 months; Waste and Transport agency costs £987k against employee savings of £526k
findings.quote: Workforce turnover has been significant, with approximately 20 –25% of the refuse workforce leaving the organisation over the past 12 months.

findings.headline: Overtime in Operational Services is reported down circa 87% in September and October compared with August claims
findings.detail: The paper attributes the reduction to Waste Team Supervisors strengthening the overtime authorisation and claims process after an Internal Audit review, which the paper says improved compliance and reduced unplanned overtime claims.
findings.matters: The paper links a specific internal audit finding to a measurable reduction in overtime spend, which a finance officer elsewhere dealing with overtime controls would find directly comparable.
findings.figures: circa 87% reduction in overtime; September and October compared with August
findings.quote: Overtime usage has reduced by circa. 87% in September and October when compared to the claims in August

findings.headline: Refuse collection (Household Waste Collection) is forecast £389k adverse, with agency costs of £216k and van and RCV hire of £175k cited
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Household Waste Collection overspend to net agency costs from staff sickness and vacancies, and to vehicle hire. It reports six hired vehicles returned in Q2 with a further RCV due back in Q3, and a new hire supplier procured at more competitive rates. The Operational Services Improvement CAT is cited as supporting issue resolution.
findings.matters: Refuse collection is a statutory service, and the paper shows agency and hire costs being reduced in-year through specific fleet and supplier actions that peers managing similar fleet problems would compare against.
findings.figures: £389k adverse variance (Household Waste Collection); £216k net agency costs; £175k vehicle hire; six hired vehicles returned in Q2
findings.quote: with six hired vehicles returned during Q2 and a further RCV planned for return in Q3

findings.headline: General Fund forecast at Q2 is a £328k deficit against a balanced February 2026 budget, a movement of £328k, with £784k of net transfers from earmarked reserves included in the forecast
findings.detail: The paper reports that the General Fund forecast outturn at Quarter 2 is an increased deficit of £328k, and that the forecast includes net transfers from earmarked reserves of £784k for grant-funded and externally contributed projects. Planning and investment income is reported as £601k more favourable, offsetting spend projected £929k higher.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to know how much of an in-year General Fund movement is being met from reserve transfers rather than the revenue base, and how far the council is relying on planning and investment income to hold the position.
findings.figures: £328k deficit; £784k net transfers from earmarked reserves; £929k higher spend; £601k more favourable planning and investment income; 1.46% increase in net spend
findings.quote: The forecast outturn position at Quarter 2 on the General Fund is an increased deficit of £328k.

findings.headline: Beyond three-year settlement to 2028/29, material uncertainty over funding from Fair Funding Review and business rates reset not yet detailed by government
findings.detail: The council operates under a three-year local government funding settlement announced February 2026, providing certainty to 2028/29. Beyond that point, the MTFP for 2029/30-2030/31 relies on assumptions from specialist advisors (Pixel Financial) because the Fair Funding Review reforms and business rates baseline reset are still being designed by government. The council's planning assumes funding may not increase in line with inflation and demand growth. It notes that 'changes to national distribution methodologies could materially affect the Council's resources', creating material planning uncertainty in the final two years covered by the MTFP.
findings.matters: Multi-year settlements provide planning certainty; loss of that certainty beyond year 3 creates long-term planning risk. If future funding falls short of assumptions, the council faces urgent deficits at a point when capacity to respond is constrained by the new unitary structure.

findings.headline: 2027/28 is final year of independent budget-setting before merger into unitary authority on 1 April 2028; decisions must avoid creating financial liabilities for successor
findings.detail: The council faces reorganisation into a new unitary authority with vesting on 1 April 2028. This makes 2027/28 the final year for sovereign budget-setting. The report frames decisions as carrying 'dual responsibility': balancing current service delivery with the imperative to avoid creating preventable financial pressures for the new authority. Budget-setting principles explicitly require proposals to 'avoid unnecessary future commitments' and 'leave a strong position for the new authority'. This creates a governance tension between responding to current needs and financial stewardship for the transition.
findings.matters: Mergers create organizational risk and final-year budget cycles often see service deterioration, control erosion, or unfunded liabilities passed forward. How well a council manages this tension is material to the resilience of the successor authority.
findings.figures: Vesting date 1 April 2028; 2027/28 is final sovereign budget-setting year
findings.quote: 2027/28 is the final year of sovereign budget setting ahead of local government reorganisation. Every decision carries a dual responsibility, therefore the Council has to balance meeting the needs of our residents, while maintaining a sustainable financial position.

findings.headline: £14.1m Sustainable Finance Programme scheduled over five years with only £630k delivered to date; delivery risk elevated by local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council's five-theme Sustainable Finance Programme targets £14.1m cumulative savings and income over 2026/27-2030/31, with commercial/income opportunities accounting for £9.9m (the largest element). Only £630k has been achieved or included in the 2026/27 budget, leaving £13.5m for future years. The programme timeline has been reshaped by local government reorganisation, with unitary vesting planned for April 2028. The report notes that reorganisation creates capacity pressures, implementation costs, and structural uncertainty that affect both timing and deliverability of the remaining £13.5m.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on realizing substantial future savings. Delivery risk is acute because the majority of the programme is scheduled for years 2027-2031 (the same period as the merger transition), meaning competing demands on officer capacity at the point when savings are most critical.
findings.figures: £14.1m total programme target; £630k achieved/in budget 2026/27; £13.5m future delivery required; commercial/income £9.9m, transformation £771k, asset management £594k, managing spend £1.2m, treasury £1.0m
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation, with vesting day anticipated in April 2028, is reshaping the SFP's planning horizon and delivery priorities. The programme must support both continued financial sustainability and a stable financial legacy for the new Unitary Council.

findings.detail: The Board identified and delivered £1.655m in savings: service development reviews (£351k), vacancy savings (£253k), commercial income (£258k), and new opportunities (£795k). The Board is continuing to play a critical role for 2027/28, focusing initially on opportunities identified in the 2026/27 process but held pending political direction, plus new opportunities to be identified during the budget setting process.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's ability to locate and deliver savings when facing budget pressures, and indicates whether the savings base is sustainable or dependent on non-recurring opportunities such as vacancies.
findings.figures: Total £1,655,766 comprising: service reviews £350,557; vacancies £252,615; commercial income £257,972; new opportunities £794,622
findings.quote: £1.65 million of savings delivered to address the predicted budget gap for 2026/27. As a result, the budget for 2026/27 out turned a balanced budget position.

findings.headline: First-quarter 2026/27 forecast shows £227k deficit versus £634 budgeted, with service overspends offset by higher planning income
findings.detail: At Q1, the council forecasted a full-year deficit of £227,134 compared to the £634 budgeted, a variance of £226,500. The overshoot reflects service expenditure pressures being partially offset by additional planning income above budget. This in-year pressure triggered the need for corrective action by the Budget Optimisation Board. The revised MTFP subsequently shows a £102,635 position for the year, suggesting further adjustments have been factored in.
findings.matters: Early-year variances indicate whether budget assumptions about service costs and income are realistic. Persistent service overspends signal structural spending pressures that savings programmes must address.
findings.figures: Q1 forecast deficit £227,134 vs budget £634; variance £226,500; revised full-year forecast £102,635
findings.quote: The current forecast position on the General fund for 2026/27 is a deficit for the year of £227,134 compared to a budgeted deficit position of £634. The main variations to budget are overspends in service expenditure, being offset by additional planning income.

findings.headline: Five-year general fund deficit forecast reduces from £21.4m to £17.5m between February and September 2026 MTFP updates
findings.detail: The medium-term financial plan was updated based on first-quarter 2026/27 performance and revised economic forecasts. The five-year cumulative deficit improves by £3.9m, driven by changes to assumptions on government funding, transitional funding under the Fair Funding Review transition, and specific grant schemes. Improvements are concentrated in later years (2029/30-2030/31), while 2026/27 shows a modest deterioration of £102k. However, beyond the current three-year settlement to 2028/29, significant uncertainty remains as the Fair Funding Review and business rates baseline reset are still being designed.
findings.matters: Finance directors monitor whether the medium-term trajectory is improving or deteriorating, and whether improvements are durable (actual resource changes) or temporary (revised assumptions that could reverse). This council shows improvement in the plan but concentrated in uncertain years.
findings.figures: £21.4m deficit (February 2026) revised to £17.5m (September 2026); improvement of £3.9m; 2026/27 worsened by £102k
findings.quote: Table 1 shows the movement over the 5 year period from the MTFP reported in February 2026 to the revised MTFP folloing a review of assumptions.

findings.headline: Multiple audit recommendations remain overdue, with moderate and low-risk issues still outstanding from 2021/22.
findings.detail: The report notes that some audit action due dates have passed, with revised dates now being tracked. Moderate and low-risk governance and control issues dating back to 2021/22 remain unresolved. The Internal Auditor confirmed these reflect outstanding revised actions that management continues to engage with.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit actions from over three years ago suggest the council has persistent implementation challenges in addressing identified control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Issues outstanding from 2021/22 still not closed
findings.quote: He noted that some due dates had passed and that status updates and revised action dates had been provided. He also referred to moderate and low-risk issues dating back to 2021/22.

findings.headline: Internal audit capacity remains under pressure and the council is relying on external associates to fill gaps rather than permanent staff.
findings.detail: The Internal Auditor reported that capacity had remained an issue with previous resource pressures documented. To manage this, the council developed an associate pool as an alternative to agency support, supported by Lighthouse. However, the process has been lengthy with ongoing challenges around host system access and onboarding of external auditors.
findings.matters: A resource-constrained audit function reduces the council's ability to provide comprehensive financial control assurance and detect problems in financial management.
findings.figures: Eight audits completed; 24 recommendations made
findings.quote: capacity had remained an issue and reminded the Committee that previous resource pressures had been reported. He explained that the market had been slow and that an associate pool had been developed as an alternative to costly agency support. He noted that the process had been lengthy, with Lighthouse supporting the internal shortfall, and that there had been challenges relating to access to host systems and onboarding.

findings.headline: Project management and transformation capacity gaps are now identified as organizational risk factors.
findings.detail: SR4 (Organisational/Transformational Change) now explicitly lists 'service capacity and project management capacity and capability across the organisation' as risk causes. The council is developing a Project Management Framework and revising its Transformation Work Programme for committee approval in September 2026.
findings.matters: The council is acknowledging gaps in transformation execution capacity. If project management capability cannot support both operations and LGR transition simultaneously, this creates material risk of service failure or financial mismanagement during 2027-2028.
findings.figures: Revised work programme due September 2026
findings.quote: The risk cause has been updated to include service capacity and project management capacity and capability across the organisation.

findings.headline: Staffing and resource risks are escalating as the LGR transition window approaches.
findings.detail: SR9 (Insufficient resources due to unplanned/unforeseen absences/vacancies) shows significant escalation in risk scores. The council is tasking HR to work with Heads of Service to identify potential resource implications for service delivery through 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: Rising staffing risks during major structural transition could constrain financial controls, change management, and core service delivery. For a lender, this signals potential management capacity constraints during the critical LGR transition period.
findings.figures: The inherent risk scoring has increased from 9 to 12 and the mitigated risk score increased from 4 to 9.
findings.quote: The risk score has been revised upwards to reflect the increased likelihood/impact as LGR vesting day approaches.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation confirmed for 1 April 2028 - South Derbyshire will cease to exist as an independent council.
findings.detail: SR16 is listed as a strategic risk with Chief Executive ownership. The LGR decision has been formally confirmed and the council is assessing the operational and financial impact, with revised approach and workplan to be reviewed in Q2 2026.
findings.matters: LGR is an existential event affecting the council's ability to continue operations and service existing debt. For lenders, this creates uncertainty about counterparty stability through the merger. For finance directors, it requires major planning for service transition.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: At the time of updating this report the LGR decision has been confirmed. The impact will be assessed, and the approach/workplan will be reviewed and revised during quarter 2 to reflect the confirmed position.

findings.headline: Leisure Centre and Office Project's sports hall provision expanded from four to six courts while remaining within the approved affordability envelope.
findings.detail: The Committee approved an amendment to the previously agreed facility mix to increase sports hall provision from a four-court to a six-court sports hall. The Executive Director confirmed the scheme remained within the approved affordability envelope despite this scope increase, with full financial implications to be reported to the Finance and Management Committee.
findings.matters: A material capital project has had its scope increased and the council has confirmed it remains within budget, indicating maintained project discipline and capital management relevant to lending decisions.
findings.figures: Sports hall provision increased from four-court to six-court
findings.quote: the scheme remained within the approved affordability envelope and that financial implications would be reported to the Finance and Management Committee

findings.headline: £1.5m of repurposed reserves is being allocated as an earmarked reserve to fund the Occupation Lane capital project.
findings.detail: The £427,000 capital budget for the Occupation Lane Site in Woodville will be funded from General Fund Reserves. A new earmarked reserve is to be created from £1.5m of repurposed reserves at the end of financial year 2025/26 to cover this investment.
findings.matters: This shows the council has reserves available to fund capital projects and is actively deploying them toward capital investment, rather than relying on additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £427,000 capital cost; £1.5m repurposed reserves
findings.quote: The capital costs can be met from General Fund Reserves; it is proposed to create a new earmarked reserve from the £1.5m repurposed reserves at the end of the financial year 2025/26.

findings.headline: Council is acquiring 53 new homes for £8.71m using S106 developer contributions.
findings.detail: The council is acquiring 45 homes from Gleesons at Cadley, Site D for £6,310,000 and 8 homes from Talbot Turf Developer on Etwall Road for £2,400,000. Both acquisitions are funded from S106 affordable housing monies received from previous development sites in lieu of housing provision.
findings.matters: This represents active deployment of developer contributions toward council housing stock acquisition rather than holding reserves, reflecting execution of housing strategy using third-party funding.
findings.figures: 45 homes at Cadley for £6,310,000; 8 homes at Etwall Road for £2,400,000; 53 homes total for £8,710,000
findings.quote: Council house acquisitions are to be funded from S106 affordable housing monies gained from previous sites in lieu of housing provision.

findings.headline: Council is investing £9.1m in capital projects with no increase to borrowing.
findings.detail: Three schemes totaling £9,137,000 are approved: Occupation Lane Site in Woodville (£427,000), acquisition of 45 council homes at Gleesons Cadley Site D (£6,310,000), and acquisition of 8 homes from Talbot Turf Developer on Etwall Road (£2,400,000). The council explicitly confirms these schemes do not increase planned or unsupported borrowing.
findings.matters: A council making capital investment without increasing debt demonstrates financial capacity and discipline in managing its debt position—a key concern for lenders assessing credit risk.
findings.figures: £9,137,000 total capital investment
findings.quote: The proposed schemes do not increase the Council's planned or unsupported borrowing requirement and are fully funded

findings.headline: Housing land supply has fallen to 4.9 years, below the 5-year statutory requirement
findings.detail: Following the King's Newton Lane appeal decision, the council's five-year housing land supply has reduced to 4.9 years, falling below the statutory 5-year housing land supply requirement. The council is implementing mitigation measures including review of strategic allocations in Part 1 of the Local Plan, with completion required by 31 December 2026.
findings.matters: A housing land supply below the 5-year requirement makes the council more vulnerable to planning appeals and can constrain development revenue and housing growth targets. It also indicates planning policy vulnerabilities that lenders monitor as indicators of local governance effectiveness.
findings.figures: 4.9 years (below 5-year requirement); Local Plan deadline 31 December 2026
findings.quote: the Council's five-year housing land supply has reduced to 4.9 years. Mitigating actions are in place to address this position ahead of the Local Plan deadline of 31 December 2026.

findings.headline: Depot operations business case withdrawn due to financial constraints
findings.detail: The council's project to review depot operations and secure alternative accommodation has been withdrawn due to financial constraints. The business case was originally scheduled for presentation to Finance & Management Committee in January 2026 and Council in February 2026 but has been deferred, with alternative options now to be presented in June 2026.
findings.matters: Deferral of capital maintenance projects due to financial constraints indicates the council is prioritizing immediate spending over essential asset maintenance, which raises concerns about asset condition and long-term capital liabilities.
findings.figures: Business case deferred from January/February 2026 to June 2026
findings.quote: this has been withdrawn due to the financial constraints faced by the Council. Alternative options will be presented to Environmental and Development Services Committee in June 2026.

findings.headline: Strategic financial risk rating escalated to 12 due to geopolitical impacts on fuel and utilities spending
findings.detail: The council's overall mitigated risk rating for decreasing financial resources has increased from 9 to 12 to reflect geopolitical landscape risks impacting council operations indirectly through spending on fuel and utilities. While the council has balanced its 2026/27 budget, the escalation reflects growing concerns about cost pressures via council and third-party contractor spending.
findings.matters: Escalating financial risk ratings indicate the council is facing tightening financial conditions, which directly impacts its ability to service borrowing and maintain service delivery. Lenders need to understand the trajectory of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased from 9 to 12
findings.quote: The overall mitigated risk rating has increased from 9 to 12 to reflect the geopolitical landscape during Quarter 4, 2025/26, and the potential this has to impact Council operations indirectly through spend on fuel and utilities via Council and third party contractor spend.

findings.headline: 2027/28 is final sovereign budget year before April 2028 reorganisation, creating dual pressures on budget decisions
findings.detail: The council must balance immediate service needs against creating a sustainable financial legacy for the new unitary authority. The document acknowledges this 'dual responsibility' and states budget decisions 'will influence not only current service delivery, but also the resilience, flexibility and sustainability of the future Unitary Council.'
findings.matters: Reorganisation-driven budget pressures could force decisions that create structural problems or hidden liabilities for the successor authority, affecting its creditworthiness and creating unexpected costs for existing and future lenders to the unitary council.
findings.figures: April 2028 reorganisation vesting date; 2027/28 is final standalone budget year
findings.quote: 2027/28 is the final year of sovereign budget setting ahead of local government reorganisation. Every decision carries a dual responsibility, therefore the Council has to balance meeting the needs of our residents, while maintaining a sustainable financial position. The decisions made will influence not only current service delivery, but also the resilience, flexibility and sustainability of the future Unitary Council.

findings.headline: Post-2028/29 funding is highly uncertain, affecting forecast reliability for 2029/30 and 2030/31
findings.detail: The 3-year funding settlement ends 2028/29. Beyond that, funding depends on yet-to-be-determined Fair Funding Review reforms, business rates baseline reset, council tax policy changes, and grant redistribution. This makes 2029/30 and 2030/31 forecasts speculative, representing 40% of the council's medium-term financial projections.
findings.matters: Lenders assess creditworthiness on forward forecasts. Uncertainty covering half the forecast period undermines the reliability of the council's financial plan and its ability to demonstrate sustainable repayment capacity beyond the settlement period.
findings.figures: Uncertainty applies to 2029/30 and 2030/31 (2 of 5 forecast years); combined deficits in uncertain years: £10,545,623
findings.quote: Beyond the three-year Local Government Finance Settlement period to 2028/29, there remains a significant degree of uncertainty over the level and distribution of local government funding. Whilst the multi-year settlement provides greater short to medium-term planning certainty, future years will continue to be influenced by the implementation of the Fair Funding Review reforms, the reset of the business rates retention system, council tax referendum limits and the consolidation or redistribution of existing grants.

findings.headline: Service expenditure overrunning by £226,500 in 2026/27 despite £1.65m in cost-saving initiatives
findings.detail: The 2026/27 forecast shows the council running £226,500 worse than budget due to service expenditure overspends, partially offset by additional planning income. This occurs despite the Budget Optimisation Board delivering £1.65m in savings across service reviews (£351k), vacancies (£253k), commercial income (£258k), and new opportunities (£795k), suggesting underlying cost control difficulties.
findings.matters: It indicates the council struggles to control operational spending even after implemented savings, raising concerns about deliverability of future Sustainable Finance Programme targets needed to address multi-year budget gaps.
findings.figures: £227,134 actual deficit vs £634 budgeted; £226,500 unfavourable variance; £1,655,766 delivered savings across four categories
findings.quote: The current forecast position on the General fund for 2026/27 is a deficit for the year of £227,134 compared to a budgeted deficit of £634. This is an overall increase on budgeted deficit of £226,500. The main variations to budget are overspends in service expenditure, being offset by additional planning income.

findings.headline: Regulatory cost pressures from Awaabs law and new legislation adding £21k+ to HRA repairs
findings.detail: HRA responsive repairs show £109k adverse variance 'in part due to new legislation'. Specifically, compensation payments increased £21k 'due to increases following Awaabs law'. Council notes fire contractor appointment for passive fire protection works with £400k earmarked reserve embedded in budget.
findings.matters: Unfunded legislative requirements imposing costs on housing authority. Awaabs law response suggests trend of increasing regulatory burden on social housing.
findings.figures: £21k compensation pressure from Awaabs law; £109k R&M adverse from new legislation
findings.quote: Compensation Payments - £21k adverse due to increases following Awaabs law.

findings.headline: Vehicle hire costs elevated due to fleet reliability issues in new refuse vehicles
findings.detail: £155k overspend in waste collection due to vehicle hire. Transport shows additional £122k variance including £69k diesel price pressure. Document states 'Vehicle hire costs remain above budget due to vehicle reliability issues and capacity shortfalls. Temporary vehicles have been hired to maintain service delivery while service issues with new refuse vehicles are addressed.' Spare parts costs also increased £30k 'due to damaged hire vehicle returns'.
findings.matters: Asset management issue: recently-purchased new fleet having reliability problems, forcing expensive temporary hire. Fleet replacement plan under review but no resolution timeline.
findings.figures: £155k van and RCV hire in waste; £69k HVO diesel pressure; £30k spare parts; £122k transport variance
findings.quote: Vehicle hire costs remain above budget due to vehicle reliability issues and capacity shortfalls. Temporary vehicles have been hired to maintain service delivery while service issues with new refuse vehicles are addressed.

findings.headline: Business rates funding cannot be forecast; contaminated data from appeals backlog
findings.detail: Council states explicitly: 'A business rates forecast has not been included in this report as system updates are required before the relevant information can be accurately produced.' Additionally, 'there is a significant increase in appeals due to the deadline for the 2023 listing. Therefore, the data is contaminated data due to speculation.' Position will be reviewed when system updates complete.
findings.matters: Retained business rates is a major funding stream (£3.446m budgeted). Unable to forecast in Q1 indicates either technical issue or appeals environment too volatile. Lenders need visibility of council's funding base.
findings.figures: £3.446m retained business rates budgeted; cannot be forecast
findings.quote: Furthermore, there is a significant increase in appeals due to the deadline for the 2023 listing. Therefore, the data is contaminated data due to speculation.

findings.headline: Waste and transport services recruited 2 suitable candidates from 10 HGV driver vacancies, with driver shortages causing missed collection rounds
findings.detail: Waste and transport services facing critical staffing gaps. 'Driver shortages resulted in missed collection rounds that required weekend recovery work, increasing overtime costs. Recent recruitment activity saw only two suitable candidates identified from ten vacancies, requiring the posts to be re-advertised.' Despite a recent pay increase, recruitment remains challenging.
findings.matters: Service delivery impact (missed collections) plus cost pressure (overtime and hired vehicles). Signals structural labor market challenge that won't resolve quickly.
findings.figures: 2 from 10 candidates; missed collection rounds requiring weekend recovery
findings.quote: Recent recruitment activity saw only two suitable candidates identified from ten vacancies, requiring the posts to be re-advertised.

findings.headline: 21% of operational workforce absent, driving £206k agency costs in waste collection alone
findings.detail: Household waste collection shows £391k overspend. Of this, £206k is agency staffing costs due to sickness and vacancies. Document states 'Around 21% of the workforce is currently absent, creating staffing pressures that require agency cover to maintain essential services. Attendance is being actively managed in line with Council policy.'
findings.matters: Absence rate of one-fifth of workforce is unusually high and indicates underlying HR/wellness issue. Mitigation plan (Employee Assistance Scheme) is reactive to the problem, not preventive.
findings.figures: 21% absence rate; £206k agency costs in waste alone
findings.quote: Around 21% of the workforce is currently absent, creating staffing pressures that require agency cover to maintain essential services.

findings.headline: County Council recycling credits for April-May 2026 transition period unconfirmed; if not paid, creates £178k unbudgeted cost
findings.detail: Garden waste disposal transferred to Derbyshire County from April 2026. Council's contract with Biffa extended to June to align with food waste collections. Previously received recycling credits. County has not yet confirmed whether it will pay credits for the April-May transition period. Document states explicitly: 'In the event these do not materialise, there will be an additional cost of £178k, which has not been factored into this outturn.'
findings.matters: Material unforecasted risk worth nearly 80% of current GF deficit; outcome depends on another authority's decision.
findings.figures: £178k unbudgeted cost if credits not paid
findings.quote: In the event these do not materialise, there will be an additional cost of £178k, which has not been factored into this outturn.

findings.headline: Employee pay award for general staff not yet agreed, creating unquantified cost pressure
findings.detail: Chief Officer pay was agreed at 3.3% in June. Council budgeted 3.2% for general employees across General Fund and HRA, but a decision on employees' pay award has not yet been agreed. Document explicitly notes 'there is a potential pressure in the year'.
findings.matters: Unresolved payroll cost could widen current deficits if award exceeds 3.2% assumption.
findings.figures: Chief Officers 3.3% vs 3.2% budgeted for employees
findings.quote: A decision has not yet been agreed for employees. The Council has built in 3.2% across its General Fund and HRA and so there is a potential pressure in the year.

findings.headline: HRA deficit increased by £236k to £447k total due to rental income shortfall
findings.detail: HRA was budgeted for £211k deficit. Q1 forecast is £447k deficit. Main driver is rental income £201,735 below forecast due to delayed property purchases and increased voids.
findings.matters: Housing revenue is supposed to be self-financing. Income shortfall creates wider deficit and depends on uncertain Q3 property purchase completions.
findings.figures: £236k increased deficit; £201,735 rental income adverse variance; forecast deficit £447k vs budget £211k
findings.quote: Income - Rental Income collection lower than budgeted due to reduction in assumed number of properties purchased or brought back into use along with increased voids.

findings.headline: General Fund deficit of £227k materializing from approved balanced budget
findings.detail: The February 2026 budget was balanced with zero deficit. Q1 forecast shows £227k increased deficit, representing a 1% increase in the council's net spend. The forecast outturn position is £20.75m against budget of £20.52m.
findings.matters: Early in-year deficit indicates structural pressure or unforecasted cost drivers, suggesting the balanced budget assumption was not robust.
findings.figures: £227k increased deficit; 1% increase in net spend; forecast £20.75m vs budget £20.52m
findings.quote: The forecast outturn position at Quarter 1 on the General Fund is an increased deficit of £227k.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 ANTI-FRAUD AND& CORRUPTION PLAN AND COUNTER-FRAUD PARTNERSHIP PERFORMANCE UPDATE
findings.headline: Counter-Fraud Partnership cost £52,681 in 2025-26 but recovered savings of £355,389, significantly exceeding annual running cost.
findings.detail: The partnership with Derby City Council delivered £355,389.02 total savings in 2025-26: £118,663.47 in recovered cash from customers and £236,725.55 in prevented losses. This was an increase of £40,006.91 on the previous year and substantially exceeds the partnership cost.
findings.matters: The partnership consistently delivers returns well above its cost, improving the council's financial position through fraud detection and recovery.
findings.figures: Partnership cost: £52,681; Total savings: £355,389.02 (cashable £118,663.47, value-for-money £236,725.55); Year-on-year increase: £40,006.91
findings.quote: In 2025-26 the Partnership cost the Council £52,681 and delivered total savings of £355,389.02. This in an increase of £40,006.91 compared to the previous year.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 ANTI-FRAUD AND& CORRUPTION PLAN AND COUNTER-FRAUD PARTNERSHIP PERFORMANCE UPDATE
findings.headline: Ongoing criminal case involving an agency worker engaged in undisclosed dual employment within Housing Service, with trial scheduled April 2027.
findings.detail: An agency worker engaged by South Derbyshire's Housing Service from 2021-24 was found to have simultaneously worked for another English local authority without disclosure ('career polygamy'). The other authority has pursued legal action against the individual and their fraudulent contract lasted approximately 6 months. South Derbyshire has provided information to support the prosecution and the council may be called as a witness at trial.
findings.matters: This reveals a control weakness: an unauthorised dual employment in Housing went undetected for three years, raising questions about the council's contractor and agency worker vetting processes and oversight capabilities.
findings.figures: Agency worker employed 2021-24; other council's fraudulent contract approximately 6 months; court date April 2027
findings.quote: The Council received formal notification from another English local authority concerning an agency worker who had been engaged within the Housing Service from 2021-24. The notification advised that the individual in question had been found to be engaged in "career polygamy" – simultaneously undertaking paid work for more than one employer without proper disclosure.

findings.headline: Head of Internal Audit rates governance framework at Reasonable Assurance, not High, with ongoing monitoring required
findings.detail: The council's governance framework operates with Reasonable Assurance per the 2025/26 Internal Audit opinion. This standard assurance level, plus the explicit note that a small number of areas require ongoing improvement and monitoring, indicates material weaknesses remain.
findings.matters: Reasonable (not High) assurance means identified control weaknesses exist and future audit findings are likely, which affects financial reporting reliability and audit risk.
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance level
findings.quote: Overall, the Council's governance framework continues to operate with Reasonable Assurance, as reflected in the Head of Internal Audit opinion for 2025/26, although a small number of areas require ongoing improvement and monitoring.

findings.headline: Only 11 of 18 prior-year governance improvements completed; 7 remain underway and 2 new issues identified
findings.detail: Of the 18 improvements identified in 2024/25, 11 are now complete but 7 remain underway into 2025/26. Two additional improvements were identified during 2025/26. Prior issues with asset disposals and procurement compliance for agency staff carried forward from 2024/25.
findings.matters: Slow remediation of governance gaps, plus new issues identified, suggests systemic control weaknesses that take time to resolve and may affect audit and financial reporting.
findings.figures: 11 complete of 18; 7 underway; 2 new
findings.quote: Of the 18 improvements identified in 2024/25, 11 are complete and 7 remain underway (see Table 1 in Appendix 1). Two further improvements have been identified during 2025/26

findings.headline: Procurement Contract Regulations non-compliance identified in 2025/26 for agency staffing and supplies within Operational Services
findings.detail: The council identified further instances of non-compliance with Procurement Contract Regulations during 2025/26, with specific issues in agency staffing procurement and procurement of supplies/services within Operational Services. A procurement transformation programme is underway to address these and improve compliance with statutory requirements and Contract Procedure Rules.
findings.matters: Procurement non-compliance indicates internal control weaknesses over spend and contract management, which affects financial control and may expose the council to legal or financial risk.
findings.figures: Multiple instances identified; specific numbers not given in main text
findings.quote: In addition, further instances of non -compliance with Procurement Contract Regulations were identified during 2025/26, including in relation to agency staffing and the procurement of key supplies and services within Operational Services.

news_drafts.headline: South Derbyshire's audit team faces staffing pressures with recommendations from 2021/22 unresolved
news_drafts.lead: South Derbyshire Council's internal audit team is managing staffing pressure by using external associates to fill gaps, rather than more costly agency staff. Onboarding these associates has proved lengthy, with the council facing challenges around gaining system access for the new team members. Eight audits were completed this year with 24 recommendations made. Yet audit recommendations from 2021/22 remain unresolved, with the internal auditor referring to moderate and low-risk issues with the council's controls and procedures from these earlier audits still being outstanding. These represent actions, the auditor confirmed, that management continues to work on.
